Content:
If an object moves at a constant speed for some length of time, we can calculate how far it travels using the formula

Content:
[MATH: \text{distance} = \text{speed} \times \text{time}.]

Content:
We can use this formula to determine how long it takes for two objects to meet.

Content:
For example, suppose a car leaves London for Glasgow, driving at [MATH: 70] miles per hour. At the same time, another car departs Glasgow for London, driving at [MATH: 60] miles per hour. If the distance between Glasgow and London is [MATH: 416] miles, how long until the cars drive past each other?

Content:
Let [MATH: T] be the number of hours from when the cars left to when they meet.

Content:
We fill in a speed-time-distance table for each vehicle:

Content:
| Car | Speed (mi/hr) | Time (hr) | Distance (mi) |
| London to Glasgow | [MATH: 70] | [MATH: T] | [MATH: 70 T] |
| Glasgow to London | [MATH: 60] | [MATH: T] | [MATH: 60T] |

Content:
When the cars cross paths, they will have driven a combined distance of [MATH: 416] miles. Therefore, we can set the sum of the distances equal to [MATH: 416] and solve for time, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 70T + 60T|= 416; 130T|= 416; (130T)/(130)|= (416)/(130); T|≈ 3.2]

Content:
So, the cars drive past each other after about [MATH: 3.2] hours.
